passage:
Rain hammered the bus shelter, and there was no dustbin in sight. Santosh, ten, finished his biscuit and crumpled the wrapper. A man beside him had just dropped a cup onto the road. "Everyone does it," Santosh muttered, and raised his arm to toss.
His father Eshaan calmly folded his own wrapper and slipped it into his shirt pocket. He said nothing.
Santosh saw. He held the wrapper for a moment, then pushed it into his own pocket. At home they found the bin, and Eshaan dropped his in first.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do with his own wrapper?
qa.a: Eshaan folded it and slipped it into his shirt pocket.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when he muttered 'Everyone does it', and why?
qa.a: Santosh felt comfortable tossing the wrapper, even justified, because there was no dustbin and a man beside him had just dropped a cup.

qa.q: What turning point made Santosh keep his wrapper?
qa.a: Santosh saw his father quietly pocket his own wrapper without a lecture, so he copied that instead.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been hoping when he pocketed the wrapper and said nothing?
qa.a: Eshaan may have hoped that showing was better than telling, and that Santosh would follow the example.

grounding: A child throws a wrapper because grown-ups do, and a parent who pockets the trash teaches more than a lecture.

passage:
Lavanya, nine, watched an auto driver toss a chips packet out of his window at the colony gate. The next day, after her ice cream, she dropped the stick and wrapper beside the gate, too. Her father Mohit said nothing. He bent, picked them up, and walked the twenty steps to the bin near the security cabin.
"Why did you take mine?" asked Lavanya.
"The bin is there for all of us," Mohit said. "I didn't want the gate to look dirty for the neighbours."
The next evening, holding her wrapper, Lavanya looked at the gate, then at the bin. She walked all the way over and dropped it in herself. Mohit was reading the newspaper, but his mouth twitched.

qa.q: How many steps did Mohit walk to the bin?
qa.a: Mohit walked twenty steps to the bin near the security cabin.

qa.q: What was Lavanya thinking when she dropped her ice cream stick and wrapper beside the gate?
qa.a: She was copying what she had seen the auto driver do, and felt it did not matter.

qa.q: What choice did Lavanya make the next evening, and what led to it?
qa.a: She walked to the bin and dropped her wrapper in herself, after her father quietly picked up hers and explained the bin is for everyone.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt seeing Lavanya use the bin?
qa.a: Mohit was probably quietly pleased, since his mouth twitched though he kept reading the newspaper.

grounding: A child drops a wrapper because grown-ups do, and a parent who picks up litter teaches more than a lecture.

passage:
In Johannesburg, Mei, nine, finished her lollipop at the bus stop and dropped the wrapper on the pavement. The grown-ups around her had done the same: chip packets, cans, tickets.
Her friend Lindiwe's mother saw it. She didn't say anything at first. She picked up Mei's wrapper, and then three more from the ground, and put them in her own coat pocket.
"Why are you doing that?" Mei asked.
"Because the pavement isn't a bin," Lindiwe's mother said. "I'll throw them away at home."
Mei's cheeks went pink. "But everyone does it."
"Everyone who doesn't know better," Lindiwe said.
The next day, Mei finished a biscuit and put the wrapper in her pocket. At home, she threw it in the bin, and felt oddly proud.

qa.q: Where did Lindiwe's mother put the wrappers?
qa.a: She put them in her own coat pocket.

qa.q: How did Mei feel when her cheeks went pink?
qa.a: Mei felt embarrassed, realising she had copied the grown-ups.

qa.q: What taught Mei more than a lecture?
qa.a: Seeing Lindiwe's mother quietly pick up and pocket the trash showed Mei what to do.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see Mei's littering?
qa.a: Lindiwe sees it as something people do when they don't know better, and she seems to want Mei to learn.

grounding: Outside India, a child litters because grown-ups do, and a parent who pockets the trash teaches more than any lecture.

passage:
At the school sports day in Mysuru, Leela, ten, finished her ice candy and tossed the stick onto the grass near the track. Half the parents in the stands had done the same.
Hemant Sir, the PE teacher, was walking past. He bent down, picked up her stick, then two plastic cups nearby, and slipped them into his tracksuit pocket.
Leela watched, cheeks hot. "Sir, I'll take it."
He smiled. "Thank you, Leela. The ground's our classroom too."
He didn't say more. But after the relay, Leela saw him still carrying a pocketful of wrappers to the bin.
At the prize-giving, she noticed her own mother drop a juice box. Leela picked it up and held it out. "Amma, pocket."
Her mother laughed, embarrassed, and took it.

qa.q: Where did Hemant Sir put the trash?
qa.a: He slipped it into his tracksuit pocket.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her cheeks went hot?
qa.a: Leela felt embarrassed and a little ashamed, realising she had littered like the grown-ups.

qa.q: Why did Hemant Sir's action work better than a lecture?
qa.a: He quietly showed what to do by pocketing the trash, so Leela learned by copying him.

qa.q: How might Leela's mother feel when Leela hands her the juice box?
qa.a: Her mother seems embarrassed but amused, surprised to be corrected by her daughter.

grounding: A child throws trash because adults do, and a teacher who quietly pockets it teaches more than any lecture.

passage:
Saturday. Thomas, eight, watched his father throw a chips packet out of the car window. So Thomas threw his too. His brother Jeevan, eleven, frowned but said nothing.
Tuesday. At school, the teacher showed a video of plastic in a river. Thomas thought of the chips packet. That night he asked, "Papa, where does our packet go?"
His father paused. "Onto the road, I suppose. Then the drain."
Next Sunday. On the drive to church, Papa finished his biscuits and folded the wrapper into his shirt pocket. Thomas stared.
"What?" Papa said. "You asked a good question."
Thomas put his own wrapper in his pocket. Jeevan grinned and did the same. At home, they emptied their pockets into the bin, one by one.

qa.q: What did the teacher show at school?
qa.a: The teacher showed a video of plastic in a river.

qa.q: What might Thomas have been thinking about when he asked where the packet goes?
qa.a: Thomas felt curious and worried, remembering the chips packet after seeing plastic in the river.

qa.q: What changed Thomas's habit most?
qa.a: Seeing his father fold the wrapper into his pocket taught him more than any lecture.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt when his father changed?
qa.a: Jeevan probably felt pleased and relieved, since he had frowned at the littering before.

grounding: Over a week, a child copies his father's littering, and the father's change to pocketing trash teaches more than any lecture.

passage: Jyoti, I saw you drop that chips packet at the bus stop. Don't make that face, listen. When I was eight, I did the same thing every day. The men at the paan shop threw their wrappers in the drain, so I did too. One evening my father and I were walking home from the market, and I tossed a toffee wrapper on the road. My father didn't scold me. He bent down, picked it up, folded it small and put it in his shirt pocket. Then he picked up two more that weren't even ours. He said nothing all the way home. I was so embarrassed I wanted to disappear. The next day I carried my own wrappers home. I still do. So your Yash Chacha is asking, Jyoti: whose pocket will you copy?

qa.q: Where did young Yash's father put the wrapper?
qa.a: He folded it small and put it in his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What did young Yash feel when his father picked up the wrapper?
qa.a: He felt so embarrassed that he wanted to disappear.

qa.q: At the turning point, why did the father's silent action work better than a scolding?
qa.a: Picking up the wrapper himself showed Yash exactly what to copy, so Yash changed the habit the next day without a lecture.

qa.q: How might the men at the paan shop have shaped children like young Yash?
qa.a: By throwing wrappers in the drain every day, they made littering look normal, so children copied them without thinking.

grounding: It illustrates a child who litters because grown-ups do, and a parent who pockets the trash and teaches more than any lecture.
